results.text: This is the part of the map called targeted memory work or “reconsolidation,” which refers to the way we reprocess the charged memory, reassess its significance, and integrate it in a more adaptive form, while still preserving an accurate account of what occurred. It works best when you are experiencing flashbacks to a specific event, rather than something more diffuse that brainspotting or other preceding therapies could address less specifically. The objective here is to reduce the persistence of these memories, so that they don’t continue to interfere whenever they recur.

results.text: Those therapies do show meaningful benefits for many people in terms of reducing hyperarousal, and sometimes dissociation. But there are two principal limitations to them that Peter Levine, et al. have identified. On the one hand, as Levine notes, exposure desensitization therapy can itself be re-traumatizing, which may be insufficiently represented in the positive evidence, because reasons for dropout and adverse events were often poorly or inconsistently reported. On the other hand, even when these trauma-memory approaches are effective, they are working against the body’s existing understanding by establishing new cognitive-behavioral patterns that suppress prior conditioned fear responses. That can produce a reduction of symptoms without resolving the root problem.
